name: CADS: Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography
description: A large-scale dataset of 22,022 CT volumes with complete annotations for 167 anatomical structures, representing a significant advancement in both scale and coverage for whole-body CT segmentation. The dataset spans more than 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries, capturing a wide spectrum of clinical variability including both normal and pathological cases.

rai:dataCollection: The dataset aggregates 22,022 CT volumes from 40 diverse sources, including large-scale public archives (TotalSegmentator, NLST, CT-RATE, AbdomenCT-1K), specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges (Grand Challenge, MICCAI challenges), focused research studies from TCIA, and newly contributed images and annotations. The collection spans 16 countries across multiple continents, integrating data from over 100 medical centers collected between 2007 and 2024. Geographic diversity includes Austria, Belgium, Canada, Switzerland, China, Germany, Spain, France, Israel, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, Portugal, Slovenia, Turkey, and United States.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Web API
rai:dataCollectionRawData: CT scans were collected from multiple sources: (1) large-scale public archives including TotalSegmentator (1,203 annotated volumes), National Lung Screening Trial (NLST, 7,172 scans), CT-RATE (3,134 scans), and AbdomenCT-1K (1,062 scans); (2) specialized annotation collections from medical imaging challenges via Grand Challenge and MICCAI, and focused research studies from The Cancer Imaging Archive (TCIA); (3) newly contributed images comprising manual annotations of critical organs-at-risk on the VISCERAL dataset, 484 newly acquired anonymized head CTs from Istanbul Medipol University, and 586 triphasic contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: All images were reoriented to the standard RAS (Right-Anterior-Superior) convention. Images were resampled to a uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution to balance segmentation accuracy with computational efficiency. Affine transformation matrices were simplified by removing rotation and translation components, preserving only scaling and shear. For patient privacy in newly acquired hospital head CT scans, a Gaussian filter (σ=5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing) was applied to facial regions to obscure identity while preserving structural integrity.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A three-step preprocessing pipeline was implemented: (1) reorientation of all images to standard RAS convention; (2) resampling to uniform 1.5 mm isotropic resolution; (3) simplification of affine transformation matrices by removing rotation and translation components. For intensity preprocessing during model training, intensities were scaled from the 5th to 95th percentiles to the range [0,1] with clipping for contrast enhancement.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The annotation methodology employed a multi-stage process: (1) Initial specialized models were trained on high-quality annotations from established datasets for nine anatomical groups; (2) Whole-body pseudo-labeling was performed using these specialized models to propagate annotations across unlabeled scans; (3) Automated outlier detection of pseudo-labels in shape space using neural implicit functions; (4) Multi-strategy label generation through an ensemble selection mechanism combining three complementary models (GT-flavor trained on original ground truth, Pseudo-flavor using all 22,022 images with pseudo-labels, Shape-flavor trained on reliable pseudo-labels after quality control); (5) Statistical ranking and selection of best-performing model flavor for each structure based on Dice scores and HD95 metrics; (6) Assembly of final labels with progressive merging order based on label reliability, with original ground truth annotations taking highest priority. Three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist contributed additional manual annotations to the VISCERAL Gold Corpus dataset for critical structures including spinal canal, larynx, heart, mammary glands, colostomy bag, sigmoid colon, rectum, prostate, and seminal vesicles.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Quality control was implemented through shape-informed label ranking using likelihood estimation in shape space. An auto-decoder based on implicit neural representations was trained on ground-truth multi-class segmentation labels. At inference time, unseen pseudo-labels were reconstructed with the shape prior model, and quality scores were computed using 90-percentile Hausdorff distance between observed pseudo-label and reconstruction. The lowest-scoring 10% of images were identified as anatomically inconsistent and excluded from training. Statistical tests (ANOVA, Welch's ANOVA, or Kruskal-Wallis test with post-hoc comparisons) were performed to assess significant differences between model flavors, with significance threshold p<0.05.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 167 anatomical structures per CT volume in the final CADS-dataset
rai:annotatorDemographics: Three in-house medical research assistants and one radiation oncologist (5.5 years in practice) contributed to manual annotations. Expert review for clinical validation was conducted by an experienced radiation oncologist.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net framework (version 2.5.1) with PyTorch (version 2.5.1) and CUDA 12.4. Neural implicit functions for shape-based quality control. VesselFM foundation model for rib segmentation refinement. ANTS non-rigid transformation for brain structure registration. MIM software for clinical reference annotations.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes patient demographics spanning multiple countries and populations. For newly acquired hospital head CT scans, facial regions were blurred using Gaussian filtering to protect patient privacy while preserving anatomical structure. The dataset includes various pathological conditions from oncological diseases (carcinomas, lymphomas, metastases) to COVID-19, traumatic injuries, and rare disorders.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The CADS framework aims to advance robust AI solutions in radiology and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers. Clinical potential spans multiple domains: in radiation oncology, it can streamline treatment planning through rapid organ delineation; in diagnostic radiology, it can enable automated organ volume quantification and detection of subtle anatomical changes; and for research applications, it can facilitate large-scale studies across diverse populations and conditions.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset may contain biases related to geographic distribution (16 countries represented but not uniformly), institutional practices (over 100 medical centers with varying protocols), and pathological conditions (mix of healthy subjects and various diseases). Approximately 79% of the initial collection lacks manual annotations, relying on pseudo-labeling which may introduce systematic errors. Known annotation quality issues exist in publicly available datasets like TotalSegmentator, particularly in ribs and vertebrae segmentations. The exclusion strategy in shape-based quality assessment may eliminate cases involving pathological conditions with atypical anatomical variations, potentially limiting the model's ability to learn clinically important edge scenarios.
rai:dataLimitations: Several limitations are identified: (1) The exclusion strategy in quality assessment may eliminate pathological cases with atypical anatomical variations; (2) Limited training data for certain structures (e.g., buccal mucosa appears in less than 1,000 scans with only 30 ground-truth annotations); (3) Very small organs (volumes below 0.5 mL) where standard CT resolution limits and partial volume effects impact accuracy; (4) Anatomically complex structures, particularly small glands, present challenges; (5) Facial features are intentionally anonymized, limiting applications requiring detailed facial analysis; (6) The brain mask includes all central nervous components within the skull, which may be too inclusive for certain applications; (7) The optic chiasm tends to be under-segmented; (8) The heart segmentation omits superior portions; (9) The rectum appears shorter than its anatomical extent; (10) The trachea is limited to air content without surrounding tracheal wall; (11) Vena cava needs more precise delineation.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training, testing, and validation of whole-body CT segmentation models. Specific use cases include: (1) Training foundational segmentation models for 167 anatomical structures; (2) Radiation therapy planning through automated organ-at-risk delineation; (3) Diagnostic radiology applications including automated organ volume quantification and detection of anatomical changes; (4) Research applications for large-scale population studies; (5) Anatomical landmark detection for automated measurements; (6) Cross-modality registration for CT-MRI fusion and PET-CT alignment; (7) Anatomy-guided image reconstruction for radiation dose reduction; (8) Body composition analysis through tissue quantification; (9) Automated localization of metastases; (10) Longitudinal organ tracking and personalized anatomical modeling. The dataset supports development of robust AI solutions that generalize across diverse clinical settings, patient demographics, equipment specifications, and institutional protocols.
